title: Catch one lightning bolt and a light bulb stays on for 116 days

beats.say: Catch one lightning bolt in a jar, and a 100 watt light bulb stays on for 116 days.
beats.speak: Catch one lightning bolt in a jar, and a one hundred watt light bulb stays on for a hundred and sixteen days.

head: WHY THAT
NUMBER?
beats.say: A typical flash carries 1,000 to 5,000 megajoules, says a government lightning expert. We take the low end: 1 billion joules.
beats.speak: A typical flash carries one thousand to five thousand mega joules, says a government lightning expert. We take the low end: one billion joules.

head: NOW PLUG IN
YOUR HOUSE.
beats.say: Now plug in your whole house. The average American home uses 10,791 kilowatt hours a year. One bolt runs it for 9.4 days.
beats.speak: Now plug in your whole house. The average American home uses ten thousand seven hundred and ninety one kilowatt hours a year. One bolt runs it for nine point four days.

head: NOW CATCH EVERY
GROUND BOLT IN THE US.
beats.say: Now catch every bolt that hits the ground in the lower 48 states: 20 million a year. That powers 514,832 homes for a whole year.
beats.speak: Now catch every bolt that hits the ground in the lower forty eight states: twenty million a year. That powers five hundred and fourteen thousand eight hundred and thirty two homes for a whole year.

head: NOW CATCH EVERY
BOLT ON EARTH.
beats.say: Now every bolt on Earth. About 40 flashes every second. That's 40 gigawatts, nonstop, enough for 32.47 million homes.
beats.speak: Now every bolt on Earth. About forty flashes every second. That's forty gigawatts, nonstop, enough for thirty two point four seven million homes.

head: AND EVERY
26 MINUTES...
beats.say: Add it up. Every 26 minutes, Earth's lightning releases as much energy as the Hiroshima bomb.
beats.speak: Add it up. Every twenty six minutes, the lightning on Earth gives off as much energy as the Hiroshima bomb.

head: SO WHY DON'T
WE CATCH IT?
beats.say: Back to reality. A whole flash is over in about half a second, and the next one lands somewhere else.

head: NO GRID
CAN CATCH IT.
beats.say: One lightning researcher put it simply: it's so sporadic and unpredictable that no power grid will ever harness it.
Follow Ship With Pip for more.

caption: What if you could catch a lightning bolt? NOAA lightning expert Don MacGorman puts a typical flash at 1,000 to 5,000 megajoules (National Geographic). Taking the low end, 1 billion joules, one bolt would keep a 100 watt bulb on for 116 days, or run the average American home (10,791 kWh a year, EIA) for 9.4 days. About 20 million bolts hit the ground in the lower 48 states each year (NOAA NSSL): caught, that is enough for 514,832 homes for a year. Worldwide, about 40 flashes happen every second (NOAA): 40 gigawatts nonstop, enough for 32.47 million homes, and the energy of the 15 kiloton Hiroshima bomb every 26 minutes. In reality, a flash is over in about half a second and strikes a new spot each time, and as one researcher wrote in The Conversation, it is too sporadic and unpredictable for any power grid to harness.
notes: National Geographic (Lagesse and Lavelle, 2012), quoting Don MacGorman, NOAA lightning expert: a flash carries 'from 100 megajoules to as high as 30,000 megajoules'; 'A typical range would be 1,000 to 5,000 megajoules'; a flash 'is actually made up of several strokes of lightning, enough to last nearly a half second'. We use the low end of the typical range, 1,000 MJ = 1e9 J. UIUC Physics Van: average strike one to ten billion joules; 'With one billion joules, the light bulb [100 W] will be lit for 116 days' (our calc gives 115.74, matches). NWS: 'A typical lightning flash is about 300 million Volts and about 30,000 Amps.' EIA FAQ: 2022 average US residential customer 10,791 kWh a year. NOAA NSSL FAQ: 'an average of 20,000,000 cloud-to-ground flashes have been detected every year' (contiguous 48 states). NOAA JetStream: 'lightning flashes about 40 times a second worldwide' (NASA satellite research). OSTI: Hiroshima 15 kilotons. NIST: ton of TNT = 4.184e9 J. The Conversation (fossil fulgurite article, first-person researcher): 'given its sporadic and unpredictable nature, no power grid will ever be able to harness lightning effectively'. Bulb 100 W is the UIUC example. The 40 flashes/s rate counts all flashes (cloud and ground), each taken at the 1e9 J low end; this is the hypothetical 'catch every bolt'. Hiroshima comparison is energy equivalence only.
